## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is no evidence in this search yet. In generation 0, all 84 trials across 7 worlds scored 0 on both dev and training success. So the agent is failing to learn at all; it is not a generalisation problem. The starting network can in principle compute what each action needs: the landing layer is a max over the footprint, and the check that the footprint is still missing is a min per layer. Generation 0 already tried the usual recipe, head and layout changes, and they gave no signal. This round tests only settings that were never tried: lr 3e-3, gae_lambda 0.8, clip 0.3, low entropy, n_envs 512 to 1024, short rollouts, and one PPO epoch to get the most samples. It also tests standard orthogonal initialisation with near-zero policy outputs, so the agent starts close to uniform over about 257 actions. Finally, it tests a deeper residual net that passes global context into the per-anchor head. Any nonzero result is the first signal we have.

### Round 2
All 84 generation-0 trials and all 3 trials in round 1 scored 0 dev success and 0 training success. That includes the most aggressive recipe tried so far (lr 3e-3, 1 epoch, 512 envs, lambda 0.8), orthogonal initialisation, and a head that adds global context to each placement score. With every score at zero, seed noise cannot be measured and no result tells one idea from another. To place a multi-cell brick correctly, the agent has to know its landing layer, which is the highest column under the footprint. It then has to check that the target is missing at that layer under every cell of the footprint. Features computed cell by cell cannot easily index a layer that depends on the whole footprint, which may be why precise placements are never learned. This round tests three different things: a structural head that learns a height distribution and gates per-layer features by it, a much smaller network (never tried), and a dense head added to the pooling head as a hedge in case actions do not map to grid cells as described.

### Round 3
All six trials so far scored 0 dev and 0 training success on both seeds, the same as all 84 trials in generation 0. Nothing has worked: aggressive recipes (lr 3e-3, 1 epoch, 512 envs, lambda 0.8), orthogonal init, adding global context to the head, a learned landing-layer head, a tiny network, or a dense head with no layout assumption. Because the dense and MLP heads also failed, a mismatch between action indices and grid cells is unlikely to be the main cause. More likely the policy collapses early (for example to an early DONE to avoid penalties for extra cells), or this world's reward is effectively sparse or long-horizon. Three settings are still untested: many small gradient steps per sample (64 minibatches), a long horizon for credit assignment (gamma 0.995, lambda 0.97), and maximum entropy with very large batches. This round tests each of them on a known-good network, so each result is easy to read.

### Round 4
All 9 trials in this search scored 0.000, as did all 84 in generation 0. Training success was also 0, so no idea can be ranked against another. These changes have all failed: aggressive recipes (lr 3e-3, 1024 envs, entropy 0.05, gamma 0.995, many small optimiser steps), a tiny network, orthogonal init, a learned landing-layer head, and a dense head alongside the pooling head. Changing the recipe further is very unlikely to help.

One mechanism that has not been tested: a random placement has negative expected reward, while DONE gets 0. The policy may therefore drift towards DONE before it learns to target the missing cells. A DONE bias of -2 and higher entropy never addressed this structurally.

Normalisation and weight sharing across brick types are also untried. Sharing the head across types lets every placement teach all four types at once.

This is the last round, so I test the factored-DONE idea alone, the shared normalised head alone, and both together.
